title: A real body raised
hook: the churches hold the resurrection was bodily, not only a feeling

segments.voice: Yesterday, recapitulation: every stage of life lived again, rightly, from the manger to the cross. Your line was every age healed. Who at a different stage did you meet kindly? Day one thousand eighty-seven.

A piece of broiled fish, and some honeycomb. That's what's on the table in a room in Jerusalem, on the evening of the first Easter, in Luke's telling. The disciples are terrified. Jesus is standing among them, and they're sure they're seeing a spirit. So he asks a strange, homely question: have you got anything here to eat? They hand him the fish. And Luke says, "he took it, and did eat before them." Ghosts don't eat supper. Among the signs Luke tells, one is a meal. Today's word: a real body raised.

These last days have asked what the cross does. Today the question is what Easter is. Some people today describe the resurrection as a feeling: the disciples' grief turning to hope, Jesus living on in their memory. The Gospels insist on something harder. In Luke, Jesus says: "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have." Handle me. Touch. In John's Gospel, Thomas says he won't believe until he puts his finger in the wounds. After eight days, John says, Jesus is there again: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands." The scars are still there. Raised, but recognizably the same body, wounds and all. And yet it's not simply a corpse come back. In John, he comes and stands among them when the doors are shut. Two friends walk beside him on a road and don't recognize him at first. Paul tries to name this in his first letter to Corinth: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." Christian teachers have read a spiritual body not as a body made of mist, but as a body wholly alive with God's Spirit: real, and new. And Paul doesn't treat this as a side detail: "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." And the old creeds confess not only that Christ rose, but that the dead will rise too. The Apostles' Creed calls it "the Resurrection of the body." Christians differ on how to picture a raised body. These texts all speak of a body.

Here's the practice: touch your own hands. Settle, and breathe. Rest one hand in the other. Feel the weight, the warmth, the knuckles, the lines in the palm, any scar you've collected. These hands have carried things, held people, made mistakes. In the Easter story, the hands that were wounded are the ones raised. Nothing is thrown away. Stay with your hands. If you pray, you can thank God for this body, as it is. If you don't, just let it be here, and be noticed. The bell holds the time.
A real body raised. The churches' confession that Easter is about a body: touchable, scarred, eating fish, and made new.
Your line: a body, not a ghost. Today, treat your body as part of the story: eat one meal slowly, or take one walk without your phone. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians who say the Apostles' Creed in worship confess the resurrection of the body, the Nicene Creed looks for the resurrection of the dead, and Easter Sunday celebrates Christ's bodily rising from the tomb.

notes: Luke 24:42 KJV includes honeycomb ('a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb'); some later editions omit it on textual grounds. The script mentions honeycomb as in the KJV. Confirm.
'On the evening of the first Easter' follows Luke 24:13, 29, 33, 36 (same day, evening). Confirm.
'Some people today describe the resurrection as a feeling' names a view without attributing it to any church; confirm fairness.
Gloss of 'spiritual body' as 'wholly alive with God's Spirit' is interpretive but widely taught; confirm.
Thomas: John never says he touched the wounds (20:28); the fork relies on this. Confirm.

BCP 1662 Apostles' Creed capitalization 'the Resurrection of the body': confirm exact form. The claim that the creeds are said in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches: the Orthodox use the Nicene Creed ('resurrection of the dead'), not the Apostles' Creed. The script says 'the old creeds'; confirm wording.
howItsDone softened from 'many churches' under the claims rule.

Editor pass: Luke's room is no longer 'locked' (that detail is John's: 'the doors were shut', John 20:19, 26), and the teach now credits the shut doors to John; 'he chose lunch' corrected to an evening meal ('ghosts don't eat supper'); 'eight days later' now follows John's 'after eight days'; fixed the garbled creed sentence ('that the dead will rise too'); lowercased the word in the hook.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): the narrator had stated the meaning of Paul's 'spiritual body' as fact; now framed as how Christian teachers have read it, and 'touchable' (not in Paul) dropped from that gloss. 'Of all the signs... he tells a meal' overstated (Luke also gives hands and feet); 'that's why the creeds' asserted an unsourced cause.
